To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a critical juncture in 1950 was a turning point in Turkey's democratization, but that the transition was neither linear nor irreversible, and that Turkey's democratization was a product of a combination of individual and collective actors' agency, as well as the structural factors that shaped the environment in which they operated.
Turkey's democracy has advanced towards maturation only after prosperity orientation came …
Turkey's transition to competitive politics was a process that began in the 1950s, was facilitated by the political leadership, and was made possible by the country's socioeconomic development. (61).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How did the Turkish political system change from a one party dominant system to a multi party system?
the following question: What are the factors that have led to the development of a democracy that is not only deepening, but maturing?
the question of how the Turkish Republic's political system has evolved over time and the factors that have shaped that evolution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Kemalist elite, in the aftermath of World War II, "saw the writing on the wall and decided to make the best of a bad job" (79) by embracing the transition to democracy.

the transition process was "a combination of the will of political actors to make it happen and the absence of a strong state apparatus that could have blocked the transition" (73).Chapter 4 examines the consolidation of democratic institutions and the consolidation of democracy.

Turkey's democratization was "the product of a combination of factors that included a strong and relatively autonomous state apparatus, the existence of a relatively cohesive political community, the emergence of a new generation of politicians with a democratic outlook, and the presence of an active, albeit weak, civil society" (75).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the transition to competitive politics was not only a result of a conscious choice by a small number of elites but also the product of a set of structural factors that made the choice for democratization inevitable.

the Turkish case is one where a "critical juncture" of transition to multiparty competition was followed by a period of consolidation and deepening that was interrupted by authoritarian interludes, which in turn were followed by new cycles of deepening and consolidation (Turan 2015).

the transition to competitive politics in Turkey was a process of "elite accommodation and compromise" (65) that took place within the framework of a "democratic regime" (64) that had been established by Mustafa Kemal and his allies. …
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transition to democracy is an outcome of a process that involves a series of decisions and actions taken by a variety of political actors, both domestic and foreign" (64).
the transition to competitive politics in the 1940s was a result of a "complex interplay of the actions of a few individuals, the dynamics of the party system and the political culture" (65).
the transition to competitive politics in Turkey was not a result of the "accidental" and fortuitous actions of a few key individuals, as some have argued.
